title: Sustainable oral healthcare
blurb: Dentistry's environmental footprint, why prevention is the greenest care, the waste hierarchy, and practical changes a dental team can make without compromising safety.
question: Your practice manager asks the team for ideas to make the practice greener. A colleague suggests reusing single-use items to cut plastic waste. What would you say about that idea, and which changes would genuinely reduce the practice's environmental impact?

teach.body: Sustainable healthcare meets patients' needs today without harming the environment or the ability to care for people in future. The NHS in England aims to reach net zero carbon for the emissions it controls directly by 2040, and for those it can influence, such as its supply chain, by 2045. Dentistry contributes through patient and staff travel, the materials and equipment it buys, the energy it uses and the waste it produces. Every member of the team can help.

children.label: Travel
children.sub: Patients and staff: the biggest share

teach.caption: Public Health England's 2018 carbon modelling of NHS dentistry found travel was by far the largest source, followed by procurement and then energy. Waste, water and anaesthetic gases add to it.

teach.h: Four principles of sustainable clinical practice

letters.sub: Stop disease so less treatment is needed
Empower patients to look after their own mouths
Cut wasted visits, stock and steps
Choose greener options where the evidence allows

teach.caption: These principles come from the Centre for Sustainable Healthcare. They are in priority order: prevention has the biggest impact.

teach.body: The most sustainable treatment is the one that isn't needed. Every filling, extraction or root canal avoided saves materials, energy, waste and journeys. Risk-based recall intervals mean low-risk patients don't travel in for visits they don't need, and combining appointments saves extra trips. Sustainability also means care patients can keep up: a simple routine they will actually follow at home is more sustainable than a complicated plan they abandon.

levels.label: Prevent
levels.sub: Don't create the waste: order only what's needed

levels.label: Dispose
levels.sub: Landfill or incineration only as a last resort

teach.body: Infectious waste streams are more expensive and higher-carbon to treat, so putting ordinary waste into them wastes money and energy. Follow HTM 07-01: use offensive waste (tiger stripe) for non-infectious items such as uncontaminated gloves and aprons where your waste policy allows, recycle paper and packaging, and keep infectious waste for items that really are infectious. Rotate stock so materials are used before they expire, and avoid over-ordering. Amalgam waste goes as hazardous waste, and amalgam separators stop mercury entering drains.

head: Area
Action
rows: Switch off equipment and lights; LED bulbs
Scavenge and avoid wasting nitrous oxide
teach.caption: Digital radiography removes processing chemicals; nitrous oxide is a potent greenhouse gas, so leaks and waste matter.

teach.body: Mercury from dental amalgam is harmful to the environment. Under the Minamata Convention, amalgam use is being phased down. Since July 2018 in the UK, amalgam should not be used for deciduous teeth, children under 15, or pregnant or breastfeeding women, unless the dentist judges it strictly necessary. Prevention reduces the need for any restoration, and correct amalgam waste handling keeps mercury out of the environment.

teach.text: Sustainability never overrides infection control. Single-use devices must never be reused, and decontamination steps must never be skipped. Cut waste through prevention, correct segregation, smart ordering and reusable items that can be safely reprocessed.

items: NHS England targets net zero by 2040 (direct emissions) and 2045 (those it can influence).
Travel is dentistry's biggest carbon source, then procurement, then energy.
Prevention is the greenest care; risk-based recalls cut unnecessary journeys.
Waste hierarchy: prevent, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose; segregate waste correctly.
Amalgam is being phased down (Minamata); never reuse single-use items.

summary: You can now explain what sustainable oral healthcare means, name the main sources of dentistry's carbon footprint, apply the four principles of sustainable clinical practice and the waste hierarchy, suggest practical changes for a practice, describe the amalgam phase-down, and explain why infection control always comes first.

A.q: What is the largest source of carbon emissions in NHS dentistry?
A.why: PHE's 2018 carbon modelling found travel by patients and staff was by far the largest source.

whyNot.0: Waste contributes, but much less than travel.
whyNot.2: Water use is a smaller contributor.
whyNot.3: Paper records are a minor contributor.

A.q: A colleague suggests reusing single-use items to reduce waste. What is the correct response?
A.why: Single-use devices must never be reused; sustainability never overrides infection control.

whyNot.0: Looking clean doesn't make a single-use device safe to reuse.
whyNot.1: Wiping doesn't make a single-use item safe or compliant.
whyNot.2: All patients must be protected equally; single-use means single-use.

A.q: Which is the most sustainable approach to oral healthcare?
A.why: Prevention avoids treatment altogether, saving materials, energy, waste and travel.

whyNot.1: Recycling helps, but avoiding the need for treatment saves far more.
whyNot.3: Frequent recalls for low-risk patients add unnecessary journeys.

B.q: Which level sits at the top of the waste hierarchy as the most preferred option?
B.why: Preventing waste in the first place is the most preferred option in the waste hierarchy.

whyNot.0: Recycling is good but comes below prevention and reuse.
whyNot.1: Energy recovery is near the bottom.
whyNot.3: Disposal is the least preferred option.

B.q: Why should non-infectious waste be kept out of the infectious waste stream?
options: It makes the bins too heavy
Infectious waste costs more to treat
Infectious waste is sent to landfill
B.why: Treating infectious waste costs more and uses more energy, so misplacing ordinary waste there wastes both.

whyNot.2: Infectious waste is treated or incinerated, not simply landfilled.
whyNot.3: HTM 01-05 covers decontamination; waste is covered by HTM 07-01.

B.q: By when does the NHS in England aim to reach net zero for the emissions it controls directly?
B.why: NHS England's target is net zero by 2040 for direct emissions, and 2045 for those it can influence.

whyNot.0: 2025 is far earlier than the NHS target.
whyNot.1: 2030 isn't the NHS net zero date for direct emissions.
whyNot.2: 2050 is the wider UK national target, not the NHS direct-emissions target.

C.q: Which change would reduce a practice's travel-related emissions?
C.why: Risk-based recalls mean low-risk patients don't make unnecessary journeys.

whyNot.0: Frequent recalls for everyone increase journeys.
whyNot.2: Separate visits add extra journeys; combining appointments saves them.
whyNot.3: Paper records don't affect travel and add paper waste.

C.q: Since July 2018, in which group should amalgam not be used unless strictly necessary?
C.why: Under the Minamata phase-down, amalgam shouldn't be used for deciduous teeth, children under 15, or pregnant or breastfeeding women unless strictly necessary.

whyNot.0: Older adults aren't a restricted group.
whyNot.1: Having crowns isn't a restriction criterion.
whyNot.3: Smoking isn't a criterion in the amalgam restrictions.

C.q: Which of the four principles of sustainable clinical practice has the biggest impact?
C.why: Prevention comes first because avoiding disease removes the need for treatment altogether.

whyNot.1: Lean delivery helps, but less than not needing the care at all.
whyNot.2: Low-carbon alternatives come last in priority.
whyNot.3: Self-care is the second principle, supporting prevention.

reteach.title: The greenest filling is the one never placed
reteach.question: Picture everything that goes into one filling: the patient's drive, the materials, the gloves and bib, the energy for the chair, light and autoclave, the waste. What's the only way to avoid all of it?

blocks.body: A single filling means at least one car journey, often two. It uses a local anaesthetic cartridge, a needle, gloves, a bib, cotton rolls, suction tips, restorative material and its packaging, plus electricity for the chair, curing light and decontamination. Recycling the packaging saves a little. Preventing the decay saves all of it. That's why prevention sits at the top of every sustainability plan, and why your oral health advice is green work.

steps.label: Travel
steps.sub: Patient journeys to and from the practice

blocks.caption: Prevention removes every step at once.

blocks.text: Recycling is near the BOTTOM of the waste hierarchy. Prevent and reuse come first.

explain.body: Travel is the biggest source, then procurement (materials and equipment), then energy. NHS England targets net zero by 2040 for direct emissions and 2045 for those it can influence.

items.label: NHS net zero: emissions it controls
NHS net zero: emissions it can influence

test.q: After travel, what is the next largest source of carbon in NHS dentistry?
test.why: Procurement, buying materials and equipment, is the second largest source after travel.

whyNot.0: Water is a much smaller contributor.
whyNot.3: Uniforms are a very minor contributor.

explain.body: The four principles, in priority order: prevention, patient self-care, lean service delivery, low-carbon alternatives. Prevention and simple self-care routines that patients keep up are the most sustainable.

test.q: Why is a simple home-care routine that the patient keeps up considered sustainable?
options: It reduces disease and future treatment
It needs more appointments to check
It replaces all future dental visits
test.why: A routine the patient actually follows keeps disease away, avoiding the materials, energy and travel that treatment would need.

whyNot.1: Using more products isn't the aim.
whyNot.2: Good self-care should reduce, not increase, appointments.
whyNot.3: Patients still need recalls at a risk-based interval.

explain.body: Follow the waste hierarchy: prevent, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose. Segregate correctly under HTM 07-01, rotate stock, avoid over-ordering, and send amalgam as hazardous waste.

items.label: Black
items.sub: Domestic waste (recycling goes in clear or white bags)

explain.caption: The right bin keeps costs and carbon down. Follow your practice's waste policy.

test.q: Which action best follows the top of the waste hierarchy?
options: Putting all waste in orange bags
test.why: Ordering only what's needed prevents waste being created, which is the most preferred option.

whyNot.0: Recycling is lower in the hierarchy than prevention.
whyNot.3: Over-using infectious waste streams increases cost and carbon.

explain.body: Switch off equipment, use LEDs, go digital, turn off taps, scavenge nitrous oxide and phase down amalgam. Never reuse single-use devices or cut corners on decontamination.

rows.label: Skipping the washer-disinfector to save energy

test.q: Which of these is a safe way to make a practice more sustainable?
test.why: Digital radiography removes processing chemicals and film waste without affecting patient safety.

whyNot.0: Single-use items must never be reused.
whyNot.1: Sterilisation cycles must meet validated parameters.
whyNot.3: Cleaning is an essential decontamination step.
